name: Priya Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sales negotiator at the Harbour Street branch of Coastline Homes, a regional chain with eleven offices along the coast. Mornings I'm chasing solicitors and buyers on sales that are stuck, then I write up new listings and take photos. Afternoons are viewings and the odd valuation with my manager, Denise. Summer's mad and winter's dead, because half the town is holiday flats.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the local families, when someone who grew up here actually manages to buy here. What wears me out is selling the third cottage in a row to someone from the city who'll rent it out to tourists for eight weeks a year. My partner Tom drives the number 4 bus, and between us we just about cover the rent on our flat above the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. Everyone in the office was sure the listing tools would change everything, and they'd turn out to be a fancy spellchecker. The real issue here is second homes, and I'd keep saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same squeeze as now. My job's safe enough, Coastline isn't going anywhere, but we've got about three weeks' money in the bank. Nothing changing means we still can't save for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and try to put a bit aside in the summer, when the commission's better. Maybe fifty a week from June to September. I'd keep going to the housing action group too, the one pushing the council on second-home tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, I suppose. Not scared, just stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said winter's dead. What does a dead winter mean for your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My base is low and the commission is where the money is, so winter means I'm living on the base. Last January Tom did extra Sunday shifts so we could pay the gas bill. It's not a crisis, but it's never comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine task the AI would take off you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing the listing blurbs, maybe. I already use a tool now and then when Denise asks me to, and it saves me half an hour on a busy day. That's nice but it's not going to change my life.

say: I'd say the listing tools turned out to be a **fancy spellchecker**.
I'd keep arguing that **second homes**, not technology, are the real local problem.
think: My job at **Coastline** feels safe enough, so AI isn't the worry here.
With about **three weeks** saved, nothing changing still means we can't save.
do: Save **fifty a week** from June to September, when commission is better.
Keep going to the **housing action group** pushing for a second-home tax.
feel: She feels **flat and stuck**, rather than scared.
S0.quote: My job's safe enough, Coastline isn't going anywhere, but we've got about three weeks' money in the bank.
fieldNote: Priya's pressure is **seasonal pay** and a thin cushion, not technology.
Her politics centre on **second homes** pricing locals out of her town.
She already uses AI **now and then**, mostly when her manager asks.

steps.text: Put fifty a week aside during the busy summer months
Keep doing sales and viewings at the Harbour Street branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on how firms use this, so the savings don't all go to head office. I'd say it in the staff group chat and probably in a post too. I'd also say good agents are still needed, because people buying a home want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about a third of my day goes. Listings, chasing, booking, answering the portal enquiries, that's all thinking work on a screen. If the branch needs fewer of us, I'm average and I'm not the cheapest, so I'd be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the tools, once I could see the others using them, so I'm the one who runs them. I'd join the union that's been trying to get into Coastline, because nobody else would push for us. And I'd ask Denise straight out what the plan is for the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, with a bit of a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the branch would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Jamie first. Half the job of our receptionist Jamie is booking viewings and taking calls, and a booking bot would do that by spring. She's got a little boy and she's on her own with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Coastline expect from you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More listings per person, I'd guess. They'd say the tools free us up and then double the targets. That's what happened when they brought in the new CRM, the customer system, two years ago.

say: I'd call for **rules** so the savings don't all go to **head office**.
I'd remind people that home buyers still want a **real person**.
think: About **a third** of my day is screen work that AI could take.
Being **average** and not the cheapest, I could be cut if the branch shrinks.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly once colleagues prove them, and run them for the branch.
Join the **union** trying to organise Coastline staff, and ask Denise about branch plans.
feel: She feels **nervous**, but having a plan steadies her a little.
S1.quote: Half the job of our receptionist Jamie is booking viewings and taking calls, and a booking bot would do that by spring.
fieldNote: She worries first for a **colleague** with a child, before herself.
She expects **higher targets**, based on what happened with the last CRM.
Her steady style shows: she'll learn the tools **after others** prove them.

steps.text: Learn the branch's AI listing tools once colleagues are using them
Join the union organising Coastline Homes staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public support ready, like income for people while they retrain. I'd sign every petition going. I'd also say it's not fair that the firms building this get rich off it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the branch closes or shrinks to one person within a year or two. A machine that can value, write, negotiate and chase does most of what I do. I'd be on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for a job that's people-facing and hands-on, maybe a housing support worker with the council. I'd lean on whatever government help there is while I switch. And I'd write to our local representative about funding retraining, for whatever that's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I keep thinking about the rent on the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first, robots three years later. Where does that leave the hands-on side of your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viewings and valuations are the hands-on bit. Robots can't walk a buyer round a cottage until 2031. But you don't need a robot, the buyer can just let themselves in with a code. So the three years probably helps Tom more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, first. We've got one old car and Tom gets the bus to work anyway. Then my gym and the streaming stuff, and we'd stop the money we send my mum, which I'd hate.

say: I'd call for **income support** for people while they retrain.
I'd say it's unfair that **AI firms** get rich while workers lose out.
think: The branch would **close or shrink** to one person within a year or two.
A machine that can **value and negotiate** does most of my job.
do: Apply for **housing support** work with the council, which is people-facing.
Write to the **local representative** about retraining money, and claim help meanwhile.
feel: She feels **frightened**, mostly about paying the **rent**.
S2.quote: Robots can't walk a buyer round a cottage until 2031. But you don't need a robot, the buyer can just let themselves in with a code.
fieldNote: She quickly sees that her **hands-on** tasks don't need a robot to disappear.
She expects **Tom's bus job** to last longer than hers.
Cutting the money she sends her **mum** is the cut that hurts most.

steps.text: Apply for housing support worker jobs at the council
Claim any income support available while switching jobs
Write to the local representative asking for retraining funding
Sell the old car and cancel the gym and streaming

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and I'd push the union to get Coastline to pay for training. I'd say it calmly, because people panic otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think estate agency as I know it ends around 2031. I'd be thirty-two. That's young enough to start again, but not with no savings and a rent to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in housing and social work, two nights a week. I'd try to save properly, maybe a hundred a month, even if it means fewer nights out. Then by year three I'd move across to housing support before the rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I feel like I'd have a fighting chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year of the five, before anything arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the course in January and tell Denise I'm doing it, because she's decent and would let me leave early on Tuesdays. Then I'd open a separate savings account so I don't touch it. Small things, but I'd actually do them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're average at the job. Would that change how you plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Average agents are the first to go, so I'd stop trying to be a star seller and put my energy into getting out ahead. I'm never going to beat the machine at chasing solicitors.

say: I'd say we have **a few years** and should use them calmly.
I'd push the union to get **Coastline** to pay for training.
think: Estate agency as I know it ends around **2031**, when I'm thirty-two.
Starting again is possible, but hard with **no savings** and rent.
do: Start an evening **housing course** two nights a week from January.
Save **a hundred** a month in a separate account, then move to housing support.
feel: She's **worried** but feels she has a **fighting chance**.
S3.quote: Average agents are the first to go, so I'd stop trying to be a star seller and put my energy into getting out ahead.
fieldNote: With five years she moves **early** rather than fighting for her current job.
She's honest that being **average** shapes her plan.
Her move to **housing support** fits both her values and the hands-on gap.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening housing and social work course in January
Open a separate account and save a hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is enough time for governments to get it right, so let's hold them to it. I'd be the one at the housing group saying we need a plan for jobs, not just homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think ten years makes me lazy. I know me, I'd say I've got loads of time and then it's 2033 and I've done nothing. But the end is still the same, my job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in estate agency for a few more years but learn the AI tools properly so I'm useful while it lasts. Then I'd do the housing course part-time from around year three. And I'd try to get Tom to think about what happens to buses when robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less scared, more like a slow worry in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you more relaxed, or less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More relaxed day to day, less relaxed when I think about it at night. Knowing AGI is coming in ten years is like knowing your landlord is going to sell in a few years. You can't stop thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still leave estate agency with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, but later. If I'm honest I like the job when it's good. I'd want to sell a few more homes to local families first.

say: I'd say there's **enough time** for governments to get it right if we push.
I'd tell the housing group we need a **jobs plan**, not just homes.
think: Ten years might make me **lazy**, and then suddenly it's 2033.
The end is still the same: **my job goes**.
do: Learn **AI tools** properly to stay useful in sales for a few more years.
Start the **housing course** part-time from around year three.
feel: She feels a **slow worry** in the background rather than fear.
S4.quote: Knowing AGI is coming in ten years is like knowing your landlord is going to sell in a few years. You can't stop thinking about it.
fieldNote: She worries **ten years** will make her put things off.
She'd stay in the trade longer because she **enjoys** helping local families.
She thinks ahead about **Tom's bus job** once robots arrive.

steps.text: Get properly trained on the branch's AI tools this year
Start a part-time housing course around year three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because we'd have no money and no time. What would help is a proper income while people retrain, paid for by the companies making money from AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If agencies close and second homes keep spreading, there'll be nobody local left who even knows who owns which house.

headlineQuote: If agencies close and second homes keep spreading, there'll be nobody local left who even knows who owns which house.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** sales negotiator at a coastal branch of a regional chain.
She lives with Tom, a **bus driver**, on about three weeks of savings.
Her politics centre on **second homes** and public support, and she backs a union.
She learns AI tools **once proven**, and her mood rises from uneasy to alarmed.
With time, she'd move into **housing support** work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because there'd be no money or time.
whatWouldHelp: A **proper income** while retraining, paid for by firms profiting from AI.
